title: Bounds on option prices
objectives: Derive no-arbitrage bounds on call and put prices.
Spot a quote that breaks a bound, or breaks the order of prices across strikes, and trade against it.

screens.prose: A share trades at £100.00. A dealer offers a one-year European call on it, struck at £90.00, for £105.00. The diagram shows what the share and the call are worth at expiry.
screens.question: Should anyone pay £105.00 for this call?

options.text: No: the share costs £100.00 and is worth more than the call at every price
Yes, if the share might rise a long way
options.why: You looked only at the upside. The share gains every pound the call gains, and more, for less money.

options.text: Yes: an option gives leverage, and leverage is worth paying for
options.why: Leverage comes from a low price, not a high one. At £105.00 the call costs more than the share it is based on.

options.text: It depends on how volatile the share is
options.why: Volatility moves a call's price only inside the bounds. No volatility makes a call worth more than the share.

hints.text: Compare the two lines at any price.
The share's line is above the call's line everywhere.
Sell the call for £105.00 and buy the share for £100.00. If the call is exercised you hand over the share and get £90.00.

feedback.correct: No. The share pays more in every state and costs less.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what the share and the call pay at expiry, and what each costs.

explain.text: Sell the call and buy the share: you take in £5.00 today. At expiry you deliver the share for £90.00 or keep it, so you never lose. So $c \le S_0$: a call is never worth more than its share.

screens.prose: Now the same call is offered at only £12.00. The rate is 5%. You buy the call, short the share, and lend £85.71, which grows to £90.00 in a year. The diagram shows the call with the short share and the £90.00 together.
screens.question: Fill in the totals: cash today, and what is left at expiry.

hints.text: At £110.00 you exercise the call. At £80.00 you do not.
The call pays £20.00 at £110.00. Each total is a column sum.

feedback.correct: £2.29 today, and nothing to pay later: £10.00 or £0.00 left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add each column, with money out negative.

byKey.r0c3: At £110.00 you buy at £90.00 a share worth £110.00: the call pays £20.00.
byKey.r3c1: Today you pay £12.00 and £85.71, and receive £100.00 for the share.
byKey.r3c2: At £80.00 the call is unused. You buy back the share for £80.00 with the £90.00.
byKey.r3c3: At £110.00 the call buys back the share for £90.00, which the loan pays.

explain.text: You take in £2.29 today and never owe anything later: the bold line never dips below 0. So a call cannot cost less than $S_0 - K/(1+r)^T = 100.00 - 85.71 = 14.29$.

screens.prose: So the call's price has a **lower bound**, $S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$, and an **upper bound**, $S_0$. The shaded band lies between them, for $K = \text{£}90.00$ at 5% for a year. A quote of £8.00 sits outside it.
screens.question: Drag the quote at $S_0 = \text{£}100.00$ to a price no one can arbitrage.

hints.text: Where is the band at $S_0 = 100$?
The band runs from the lower line to the upper line.
Any price from £14.29 up to £100.00 is inside the band.

feedback.correct: Inside the band, from £14.29 to £100.00, no trade is free money.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the quote between the two lines.

byKey.below: Still below the lower line. Buying the call, shorting the share and lending £85.71 would still pay.
byKey.above: Above the share price. Selling the call and buying the share would pay.

explain.text: Below the band you buy the call and hedge, as on the last screen. Above it you sell the call and buy the share. Where in the band the price sits depends on more than arbitrage: how much the share moves.

screens.prose: Same call, $K = \text{£}90.00$, but the share has fallen to £80.00. The formula $S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$ now gives a negative number.
screens.question: What is the lowest price the call can have?

hints.text: Could a call ever cost less than nothing?
Left of $K/1.05$ the lower line lies flat on 0.
$80.00 - 85.71 = -5.71$, but the holder can always walk away, so the call is worth at least 0.

feedback.correct: £0.00. A right you never have to use is never worth less than nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$ with 0, and take the larger.

byKey.negative: You kept the negative number. Nobody would pay you to take a right they need never use.
byKey.intrinsic: You used $S_0 - K$ without discounting, and kept the negative. The floor is 0.

explain.text: The full lower bound is $\max(S_0 - K/(1+r)^T, 0)$. Left of £85.71 the lower line is flat at 0; right of it, it rises with slope 1. That kink mirrors the payoff, shifted left by the interest on $K$.

screens.prose: Slide the strike $K$ and watch the band. At a strike of 0 the call is the right to take the share for nothing.
screens.question: With the share at £100.00, what is a call struck at £0.00 worth?

widget.label: Zero-strike call price
widget.accept: £100.00: the lower and upper bounds meet at $S_0$

hints.text: Set $K$ to 0. What happens to the band?
At $K = 0$ the lower line is $S_0$ itself.
Both bounds equal $S_0 = 100$: a zero-strike call is the share.

feedback.correct: £100.00. A call struck at 0 is the share itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide $K$ to 0 and read where the band closes up.

byKey.zero: You read a zero strike as a worthless call. A strike of 0 means the share costs nothing to take, so the call is worth the share.
byKey.pv: You discounted the share. You get the share itself, which is worth £100.00 today.

explain.text: At $K = 0$ the lower bound $S_0 - 0$ meets the upper bound $S_0$, so $c = S_0$. As $K$ grows the lower line slides right and the band opens. A strike far above any share price leaves a call worth almost nothing.

screens.prose: Puts have bounds too. A one-year European put struck at £110.00, on a share at £100.00, at 5%. The band is for the put: the floor is $K/(1+r)^T - S_0$, and the cap is $K/(1+r)^T$.
screens.question: What is the lowest price the European put can have?

hints.text: Mirror the call: discount the strike, then compare with the share.

feedback.correct: £4.76. Buy the put and the share, and borrow £104.76: you can never lose.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount the strike to today, then take away the share price.

byKey.american-bound: That is $K - S_0$, what exercising now would pay. A European put cannot be exercised until expiry, so discount $K$.
byKey.zero: Zero is the floor only when the share is above $K/(1+r)^T$. Here it is below.

explain.text: The floor is $\max(K/(1+r)^T - S_0, 0) = 4.76$. The cap is $K/(1+r)^T = 104.76$, the most the put can pay, discounted. An American put can be exercised now, so its floor is $K - S_0 = 10$ and its cap is $K = 110$.

screens.prose: Back to the call struck at £90.00, share at £100.00, 5% for a year. A screen shows it at £9.50, below even $S_0 - K = \text{£}10.00$. A colleague calls it a bargain and buys it to hold.
screens.question: What is the best reading of this quote?

options.text: An arbitrage: buy the call, short the share, lend £85.71, and take £4.79 today
A bargain: hold the call for the upside
options.why: You bought it and kept the risk. If the share falls below £90.00 the call ends worthless. The hedged trade takes £4.79 now whatever happens.

options.text: Fair, if the market expects the share to fall
options.why: You treated the quote as a forecast. The hedged trade wins whatever the share does, so no forecast can justify the price.

options.text: Buy and exercise at once for 50p, the only profit available
options.why: Only an American call can be exercised now, and 50p is less than the £4.79 the hedge locks in.

hints.text: Where is the quote compared with the band?
The quote is below the lower line, £14.29.
Repeat the hedge from earlier: $100.00 - 9.50 - 85.71 = 4.79$ today, and nothing owed later.

feedback.correct: A quote below the lower bound is an arbitrage, not a bargain.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A price outside the band can be traded against with no risk.

byKey.bargain: You bought it to hold, so you carry the share's risk. The hedge removes it and pays £4.79 now.
byKey.forecast: No view of the share matters here: the hedged trade never loses.

explain.text: Below the band, the hedge pays today and owes nothing later. In practice such a quote is usually stale, or there is a cost: borrowing the share, a wide spread. Bounds hold up to those frictions.

screens.prose: We found the call's floor with numbers. Now we derive it for any European call on a share with no dividend, using two portfolios as in parity.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: A call plus cash worth $K$ at expiry pays $\max(S_T, K)$, as in parity
$\max(S_T, K) \ge S_T$: it pays at least what one share pays, in every state
Paying at least as much in every state, it must cost at least as much, or we buy it and sell the share
So $c + K/(1+r)^T \ge S_0$, that is $c \ge S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$
The holder can walk away, so $c \ge 0$ too: $c \ge \max(S_0 - K/(1+r)^T, 0)$

hints.text: Start from the payoff of the call plus cash.
Compare that payoff with one share before you compare prices.
Payoff, comparison with the share, dominance, the price inequality, then the floor at 0.

feedback.correct: Payoffs, dominance, then prices, then the floor at 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the payoffs before you compare the prices.

byKey.c: Dominance needs the payoff comparison first. Put the $\max(S_T, K) \ge S_T$ line above it.
byKey.e: The floor at 0 finishes the bound. It comes last.

explain.text: The argument is parity with an inequality in place of the equality. One portfolio dominates another, so it costs at least as much. Each violation of the bound is the arbitrage that dominance gives.

screens.prose: Now the cap on a European put, $p \le K/(1+r)^T$. We argue from what a put can ever pay.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: At expiry a put pays $\max(K - S_T, 0)$
A share price is never below 0, so the payoff is at most $K$
Suppose $p > K/(1+r)^T$. Sell the put and lend all of $p$
At expiry the loan returns $p(1+r)^T > K$, more than any payout, so we keep a profit
That is an arbitrage, so $p \le K/(1+r)^T$

hints.text: What is the most a put can pay?
The payoff is largest when $S_T = 0$.
Payoff, its maximum $K$, then suppose the cap fails, sell and lend, and show the profit.

feedback.correct: The most a put can pay is $K$, so it is worth at most $K$ discounted.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the largest payoff first, then show what goes wrong if the price is higher.

byKey.c: Assume the cap fails only once you know the largest payoff, $K$.
byKey.e: The conclusion comes once the trade has shown a profit.

explain.text: A put can never pay more than $K$, so it is never worth more than $K$ paid for sure. An American put can pay $K - S_0$ today, so its cap is $K$ itself.

screens.prose: Across strikes, a lower strike pays at least as much, so $c(K_1) \ge c(K_2)$ when $K_1 < K_2$. A butterfly on $K_1 < K_2 < K_3$, equally spaced, never pays less than 0 (level 2, l7), so $$c(K_1) - 2c(K_2) + c(K_3) \ge 0.$$ Call prices fall and are **convex** in the strike.
screens.question: The 95 call costs £13.27 and the 105 call £7.97. What is the most the 100 call can cost?

hints.text: Rearrange the butterfly rule for $c(K_2)$.

feedback.correct: £10.62: the middle price is at most the average of its neighbours.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $c(K_1) - 2c(K_2) + c(K_3) \ge 0$ and solve for $c(K_2)$.

byKey.monotone-only: You used only that prices fall with the strike. Convexity is tighter: the average of the neighbours.
byKey.lowest: That is the floor from falling prices, not the cap. The question asks for the most it can cost.

explain.text: Convexity says $2c(100) \le 13.27 + 7.97$, so $c(100) \le 10.62$. Falling prices alone only cap it at £13.27. Puts rise with the strike instead, and are convex too.

screens.prose: A market maker's screen shows one-year European calls on a share at £100.00. One quote breaks the rule you just used. Check each middle strike against its two neighbours.
screens.question: Tap the row with the mispriced quote.

hints.text: For each middle strike, compare its price with the average of its neighbours.
Check 100: the average of £13.27 and £7.97 is £10.62.
£11.20 is above £10.62, so the 100 call is too dear. The others pass.

feedback.correct: The 100 call, at £11.20, is above the £10.62 that convexity allows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each middle strike: is it at most the average of its neighbours?

byKey.r0: The 90 call is the dearest, as the lowest strike should be. Test the middle strikes.
byKey.r4: The 110 call is the cheapest, as the highest strike should be. Test the middle strikes.
byKey.low-strike: The 90 call is the dearest, as the lowest strike should be. Test the middle strikes.
byKey.high-strike: The 110 call is the cheapest, as the highest strike should be. Test the middle strikes.

explain.text: At 100 the average of the neighbours is $(13.27 + 7.97)/2 = 10.62$, below the quote of £11.20. Prices still fall with the strike, so only convexity catches it.

screens.prose: Trade against the 100 call: buy one 95 call, sell two 100 calls, buy one 105 call. That butterfly pays at least 0 at expiry, as in l7.
screens.question: How much cash do you take in today?

hints.text: Selling brings cash in; buying sends it out.
You sell two 100 calls for £11.20 each.

feedback.correct: £1.16 today, and a payoff that is never negative: pure profit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two sales and take away the two purchases.

byKey.one-call: You sold only one 100 call. The butterfly sells two.
byKey.sign: You have the sign the wrong way. You receive more for the two sales than you pay for the two purchases.
byKey.half: You halved the credit. Each butterfly takes in the full £1.16.

explain.text: You take in $22.40 - 13.27 - 7.97 = \text{£}1.16$ today. At expiry the butterfly pays between 0 and £5.00, so you can only gain more. A model that output these prices would fail this check.

ideas: A call is worth at most the share, $c \le S_0$, and at least $\max(S_0 - K/(1+r)^T, 0)$.
A European put lies between $\max(K/(1+r)^T - S_0, 0)$ and $K/(1+r)^T$; an American put's cap is $K$.
Across strikes, call prices fall and are convex: a butterfly never costs less than 0. Every broken bound is an arbitrage.

formula.name: Call bounds
formula.note: A zero strike makes both sides $S_0$: the call is the share.

summary.trap: A call below its lower bound is not a bargain to hold: hedge it, and take the profit with no risk.

quiz.prose: A share trades at £50.00. A one-year European call is struck at £40.00, and the rate is 4%.
quiz.question: What is the lowest price the call can have?

byKey.intrinsic: You used $S_0 - K$. The strike is paid in a year, so discount it: $40.00/1.04 = 38.46$.
byKey.zero: Zero is the floor only when $S_0$ is below $K/(1+r)^T$. Here the share is well above it.

quiz.prose: A new pricing model values one-year European calls on a share at £100.00, struck at £90.00, at 5%. Four runs with different volatilities give these prices.
quiz.question: Which output proves the model has a bug?

options.why: You picked a typical price. £16.62 sits inside the band from £14.29 to £100.00.
You thought a high price impossible. Very high volatility can push a call up towards the share price, £100.00.
You read a price near the share as impossible. Only a price above £100.00 breaks the cap.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the floor $S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$ first.

explain.text: The floor is $100.00 - 90.00/1.05 = 14.29$. No volatility can take a price below it, so £14.00 means a bug. Bounds are a cheap first test for any pricer.

quiz.prose: A put struck at £100.00 expires in a year. The rate is 5%.
quiz.question: What is the most an American put can be worth, and the most a European one can be worth?

options.why: You discounted for both. An American put can be exercised at once, when the share is near 0, and pay nearly the full £100.00 now.
You swapped them. The European put pays at expiry, so its cap is discounted.

options.text: Both are capped by the share price
options.why: That is the cap on a call. A put's payoff is capped by its strike.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask when each can pay the most it ever pays, $K$.

explain.text: Either put pays at most $K$. The European one pays it only at expiry, so it is worth at most $100.00/1.05 = 95.24$. The American one could pay it now.

quiz.prose: A screen shows one-year European calls on one share: the 100 call at £10.39 and the 105 call at £10.80.
quiz.question: You buy the 100 call and sell the 105 call. How much do you take in today?

feedback.correct: £0.41, and the spread never pays less than 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the sale price less the purchase price.

byKey.sign: You have the sign reversed. You sell the dearer 105 call and buy the cheaper 100 call.

explain.text: A bull spread, long 100 and short 105, pays between 0 and £5.00 at expiry. Here you are paid £0.41 to hold it. Call prices must fall as the strike rises.
